app: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)

functionalObligations.text: A customer withdrawing BTC (or DOGE, XRP, ADA, LTC, MEGA) from a Coinbase account to a supported network receives a 1:1 wrapped ERC-20 instead of the native asset: cbBTC on Base, Ethereum, Solana and Arbitrum, and cbDOGE, cbXRP, cbADA, cbLTC, cbMEGA on Base.
functionalObligations.note: APPROXIMATE at the level of law L9 (Xf -> debit(source) = credit(destination)). The credit is a mint and is observable; the debit is a ledger entry inside a company and is not, so the law's equality has one observable side and one asserted side. Xf presumes a source-domain transaction; here there is none.

functionalObligations.text: What secures the peg is that Coinbase holds the underlying asset and continues to unwrap on demand; there is no message, no proof, no verifier set and no threshold anywhere in the system.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, category headline confirmed for the second of three custodial wrappers. VERIFICATION-MODEL AXIS: single-company attestation, and here minting is an operational decision rather than an attested event. Xm must not be assigned. As with WBTC, law L8 discharges Xf by a 'named custodian' branch that is not an element.

functionalObligations.text: No contract escrows the underlying on any source chain, and five of the six source assets live on chains that cannot run a verification contract at all -- Bitcoin, XRP, Dogecoin, Cardano and Litecoin -- while the sixth, MegaETH, can.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS: custodial wrap. The corpus residue says this bridges five non-smart-contract source chains; it is now five of six, cbMEGA being the exception, so the claim needs the qualifier. The vocabulary's cross-domain group assumes both domains can execute code, which is false for five sixths of this application.

functionalObligations.text: The conversion is a side effect of a transfer rather than a transaction the user submits: the user asked to withdraw BTC, and the system delivered cbBTC; sending the wrapped token back to a Coinbase account auto-unwraps it.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. No element for a domain crossing that the user does not initiate and cannot decline at the point of transfer.

functionalObligations.text: Redemption is depositing the wrapped token into a Coinbase account, which auto-unwraps it and credits the underlying asset; there is no contract-level redemption and no order book or trading pair for the wrapped token on Coinbase.
functionalObligations.note: APPROXIMATE, same overstatement as WBTC F7: redemption is an account action governed by the User Agreement and gated by account standing, not a contract right, and non-customers have no redemption path at all. Rd asserts a right and cannot say who holds it or under what terms it is withdrawn.

functionalObligations.text: The redemption right is conditioned on jurisdiction and asset: cbBTC cannot be sent or received by accounts in Canada, Japan and Georgia, and the other five wrapped assets are blocked in over a hundred jurisdictions including most of the EEA, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong and New York State.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Rd cannot carry a jurisdiction vector and Aw gates access, not redemption. Law L26 (Aw + Xf -> destination-enforced eligibility + revocation propagation + jurisdictional binding) is the nearest rule and points the wrong way: it demands enforcement at the destination, whereas this eligibility is enforced at the issuer's account layer, invisible to every contract in the construction. The same token has a redemption right in one country and not in another.

functionalObligations.text: The issuer publishes a live per-address proof of reserves -- 96,065.18 BTC of reserve against 96,054.41 cbBTC of supply, 20 reserve addresses, refreshed 8/4/2026 8:45 PM, split 48,338.78 / 44,528.809 / 3,108.551 / 78.272 across four networks -- and the Ethereum-side supply reads 48,338.77958531 cbBTC on chain, matching the first bucket exactly.
functionalObligations.note: APPROXIMATE against law L27 (At -> named attester + independence + stated assurance + staleness bound + recourse): there is an attester (the issuer, not independent), a timestamp, no assurance level and no recourse. CORPUS DEPARTURE: the corpus marker calls the reporting 'periodic'; it is a live per-address feed with a machine-readable JSON endpoint, plus a reported Chainlink Proof of Reserve feed on Base and Ethereum (third-party source only, chainlink social post, not a first-party Coinbase page). Still issuer-published, but 'periodic' is no longer accurate. At launch on 2024-09-12 the issuer said proof of reserves 'will follow'; it now exists, including per-asset pages for the other wrapped assets.

functionalObligations.text: Third parties treat the issuer's own reserve JSON as ground truth for the protocol's size: DefiLlama's adapter calls getConfig('coinbase-cbbtc-proof-of-reserves', 'https://www.coinbase.com/cbbtc/proof-of-reserves.json') and sums the declared addresses.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. At names an attestation; it cannot name the circularity in which the measured value of a $6.16b protocol is the issuer's own file. RANKING BASIS: DefiLlama coinbase-bridge = $6,162,585,917 against the corpus's $6,150.9m, of which $6,158.1m (99.93%) is cbBTC -- rank #3 stands and the entry is de facto a cbBTC entry.

functionalObligations.text: Issuance authority is a chain of on-chain roles: an owner appoints a masterMinter, which grants and revokes per-minter allowances; on Ethereum owner = 0xce56d20689d836ec7a728ceb94a15746696c16e6 and masterMinter = 0x1302dfb1f806398f48650c75ab0fda9a0186f47b.
functionalObligations.note: APPROXIMATE. Aw is a user-facing permission gate as written; here it is a registry of permitted issuers with per-party allowances -- the same issuer-side reading the corpus marks for CCTP. It is a weaker instance than WBTC's Members registry, which enumerates 47 counterparties and a custodian.

functionalObligations.text: Minting is rate-limited with programmatic allowance replenishment: a MintForwarder contract lets a minter continuously mint up to N tokens over M time without a cold masterMinter key having to top the allowance back up.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. A bounded issuance rate is a genuine safety mechanism -- the only quantitative bound on any authority in the three custodial wrappers -- and no element names it. The nearest shapes in the vocabulary are Wq (rationing exits) and Ep (epoch boundaries), and neither is a rate limit on a privileged action.

functionalObligations.text: A named blacklister role -- 0x5130bf38bf5342aa06cc79b8cc198cce832b01af -- can blacklist and un-blacklist any address, blocking that holder's transfers at transfer time.
functionalObligations.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Fz), and a firm assignment rather than a marker: Coinbase is the ONLY one of the three custodial wrappers with an on-chain freeze. Two elements are listed because both genuinely discharge it and the vocabulary gives no rule for choosing: Fz names the power, and Aw under law L16 names exactly this mechanic ('transfer-time enforcement where eligibility follows the holder'). Law L28 (Fz -> named authority + enumerated triggers + appeal path + holder disclosure) has one of four: the authority is named, the triggers, appeal and disclosure are not.

functionalObligations.text: A named pauser role -- 0x1ac78dfcae082e9fe286d1ccb12c17a3e906b906 -- can halt all transfers of the token; paused() is currently false.
functionalObligations.note: Gp is correct. As with WBTC, it does not distinguish a pause over all holders' transfers from a pause over new issuance.

functionalObligations.text: The token's implementation can be replaced outright: cbBTC is a FiatTokenProxy exposing upgradeTo, upgradeToAndCall and changeAdmin, currently pointing at FiatTokenV2_1 at 0x7458bfDC30034EB860B265E6068121D18Fa5Aa72 (solc 0.6.12), the same implementation address on Base and Ethereum, held in the legacy ZeppelinOS slot 0x7050c9e0... rather than the EIP-1967 slot, which reads zero.
functionalObligations.note: Up is right and is the load-bearing difference between this entry and the other two custodial wrappers: nothing in WBTC or BTCB is comparable. Law L15 (Up -> Tg | bounded emergency process) is NOT satisfied -- see F14 -- and that failure is the finding, not a defect of the decomposition.

functionalObligations.text: The holders of these powers are single keys: eth_getCode returns empty for both owner and masterMinter, so there is no multisig contract and no timelock anywhere in the admin surface.
functionalObligations.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_getCode(owner) and eth_getCode(masterMinter), both empty (accessed 2026-08-04)
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, and the correction the corpus most needs. Giving Coinbase Up and withholding Tg gets the direction right for the wrong reason: it is not that the issuer chose upgradeability over delay, it is that there is no delay and no quorum at all. Prohibition X9 ('Up with immediate single-key control', class H) is precisely this shape and cannot be evaluated, because the vocabulary has no way to state that the holder of an element is one key -- and the holder type of the proxy admin specifically was not read on chain, so X9's antecedent remains unverified even for a human reader.

functionalObligations.text: Authority is partitioned across keys: the owner can change owner, pauser, blacklister, masterMinter and oracle, and cannot change the proxy owner, so upgrade authority sits behind a separate key from role administration.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Control elements are unary predicates on a protocol; there is no way to state that two of them are held by different parties, which is the difference between one compromised key ending the system and one compromised key degrading it.

functionalObligations.text: The contract that holds every balance is not the issuer's own code: the repository states the token 'will be an exact duplicate of centre-tokens [FiatTokenV2_1]' and the proxy an exact duplicate of the centre-tokens proxy, and the issuer's repository has not been touched since 2023-05-12 and never mentions cbBTC or any of the newer wrapped assets by name.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. No element for provenance: that the security-relevant source is a third party's, that the issuer's own repository documents a different product, or that the repository declares MIT in package.json with no LICENSE file at the root. Byte-comparison against centre-tokens v2.1.0 was not performed.

functionalObligations.text: The custodian of the underlying is also the largest venue on which the underlying trades, so the party whose failure would break the peg is the same party whose order book would price the break.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. A concentration property with direct depeg implications and no symbol; the nearest thing in the algebra is prohibition X3 (protocol token as collateral and oracle market and backstop), which is the same reflexivity worry stated only for a protocol's own token.

functionalObligations.text: One reserve pool backs four networks' supply of cbBTC simultaneously (48,338.78 Ethereum, 44,528.809, 3,108.551 and 78.272 on the others), reconciled only on the issuer's page.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. No element for a single reserve drawn against by several representations on different domains -- the same shape as BTCB's three representations. A per-chain supply is checkable, the aggregate against reserve is not, and only the aggregate is the peg.
